text.p: Cemex earnings per share are expected to fall well short of their 1995 performance when the Mexican cement giant's 1996 results are reported in the first week of March.
A Reuters survey of eight analysts who covered Cemex showed an average EPS forecast of 5.40 pesos for 1996, down from 7.10 pesos in 1995.

Analysts expect the operating margin for all of the Monterrey-based Cemex's units worldwide for the fourth quarter and the year to come in at around 24 percent, which would be up one percentage point from the fourth quarter of 1995 and unchanged for the year as a whole.

Sales volumes in Mexico are expected flat to slightly higher for 1996 versus 1995, with fourth-quarter estimates ranging from 3.41 million to 3.8 million tonnes. Domestic tonneage in the third quarter of 1996 was 3.37 million tonnes.

Strength in the company is seen in its Mexico operations while doubt clouds some of Cemex's foreign ventures, such as the Colombia unit, which will likely see its margins squeezed because of the consolidation of Cementos Samper. Spanish results also could prove weak.
Cemex, which says it is the world's fourth largest cement company, also has cement assets in Venezuela, the United States, Panama and the Dominican Republic.

"The earnings report should be fine in Mexico, and I think that the consolidated numbers will be in line with expectations without being extraordinary," said Gordon Lee, an analyst with Deustche Morgan Grenfell in Mexico City.
Analysts anticipate that net profits will appear lackluster because of distortions from the monetary position and foreign exchange losses.
For some, the more telling figure will be the operating margin, which is expected to hold steady even though Cemex reduced prices during the fourth quarter.
The average realized price per tonne sold in Mexico during the fourth quarter was $73.50 compared to about $79 in the third quarter, according to the survey of analysts.

"The strategy of maintaining competitive prices in Mexico during the second half of 1996 should not affect operating margins in a significant way," said Gerardo Saenz of the OBSA-GSerfin brokerage in Mexico City.

However, Sobani Warner of Bear Stearns in New York said the lower prices raised concerns at one point "but I think that the market has anticipated that and knows that margins for cement companies could come down."
In any event, Cemex decided to eliminate the discounts effective in first quarter of 1997, raising domestic wholesale prices by 15-20 percent in nominal peso terms.

"Generally speaking, at this time I see that sales volumes in Mexico should be better than they were in the third quarter of 1996 and the fourth quarter of 1995," said Eric Linder of JP Morgan in New York.
More than the price discounts, higher energy costs are seen cutting into profits for the Mexican operation, some analysts said.

Analysts expect a significant increase in the sales volumes of ready-mixed concrete during the fourth quarter, which would signal a recovery in the formal construction sector not seen in the previous quarters.
"I think the market will react very positively to the increase in ready-mixed concrete," said Carmen Slade of Salomon Brothers in New York. "I think that it will be an important focus for 1997."
